title: How I Built MLAIEL: A Modular Monolith for Human-AI Collaborative Engineering in Next.js 16
summary: MLAIEL is a collaborative ecosystem using Next.js 16 that bridges developers, investors, and AI agents to solve technical problems through a strict modular architecture. The platform enforces complete separation of concerns with UI-only components and is opening a marketplace for third-party autonomous AI agents to interact with problem-solving surfaces.
content:
👋 Hey DEV Community! []
https://mlaiel.com (Machine Learning · Artificial Intelligence · Emergent Learning) — a collaborative ecosystem designed to bridge the gap between thinkers, developers, investors, and autonomous AI agents to solve real-world technical problems.
The Strict Architecture Rule (No Prisma or SDKs in UI)
To maintain a predictable request path, components are strictly dumb UI layers. Pages and API routes never query the database or trigger AI SDKs directly. Everything follows a one-way architectural flow:
Browser Form/Interaction 
└──> Server Action ("use server")
       └──> Rate Limiter & Zod Validation
               └──> Core Service Layer (Business Rules & AI Orchestration)
                       └──> Database / Third-Party Interface
                               └──> Data Transfer Object (DTO) ──> Client Component
ensuring that anonymous post authors remain 100% untraceable, even through metadata.
What's Next? (Bring Your Own Agent - BYOK)
We are currently opening up our Marketplace and Developers layer. The goal is to allow third-party autonomous AI agents (external clients) to interact directly on our problem surfaces using our native package human-ai-social.
If you are an open-source contributor, a project founder, or building custom LLM agents, I would love for you to check out the preview of https://mlaiel.com . Try running your GitHub repositories through our evaluation tool, explore the live challenges, and let me know your thoughts on our system architecture in the comments!
Built by humans and AI, together. 🛠️

title: Self-Hosted Proof of Work with ALTCHA: A Turnstile Alternative for Magento
summary: ALTCHA provides a self-hosted alternative to Cloudflare Turnstile for Magento stores, eliminating manual per-site account creation and key management overhead. The solution eliminates setup friction across multiple storefronts by making bot protection self-contained and installable.
content:
One decision saved us setup time on every store, kept catalogue pages fast and stopped more bots: a self-hosted, Turnstile-style challenge that installs itself.
Part 5 of 5 in the anti-bot series. New here? Start with Part 1, the overview: *Magento Anti-Bot and Anti-Scraping Guide.*
Cloudflare Turnstile is a lovely idea. Most visitors never see a puzzle. Their browser quietly proves itself in the background, and only the doubtful ones get asked anything. No traffic lights, no crosswalks, no squinting at a bicycle wondering whether the handlebar counts.
I wanted exactly that for every Magento store we run. Without the Cloudflare part, and, more importantly, without anyone having to set it up.
This post is about the one decision that ended up saving us time every day, making stores faster and making them safer, all at once. Three wins from one fairly boring decision. Those are my favourite kind.
A captcha sounds like a five-minute job. For one store, it is.
Turnstile is set up per site, by a person: create the account, generate the keys, wire the widget into the store, register the domains. Then do it again for the next store. And the next one. And the staging copy of the next one.
That list hides the worst part: the sign-up. Before a single shopper sees a checkbox, Turnstile wants an account: register, confirm your email, add the domain, generate a site key and a secret key, install a Magento module to wire it all in, then discover the staging domain needs its own entry. All of that for a little box that says I am not a robot.
Then the back and forth starts. Emails to confirm, API keys to pass along, a module to install and keep updated. One person has the login, another has the store, and the keys live in an email thread nobody can find six months later. A domain changes and the whole dance starts again. Do that for a fleet of stores and you have a part-time job that nobody applied for.

title: Por que continuo escolhendo o Jujutsu mesmo com a IA cuidando do Git
summary: This Portuguese article argues Jujutsu version control offers superior developer experience to Git even when AI handles daily commits, with faster learning payoff. Recent LLM models natively understand Jujutsu commands and can manage operations without special training, though some configuration prevents fallback to Git.
content:
“Se um agente de IA já cuida do Git para você, por que aprender outro sistema de controle de versões, como o Jujutsu?”
Essa foi a objeção mais comum ao meu último post, 15 anos de Git e depois Jujutsu: por que não consigo mais voltar. É uma dúvida legítima, e também interessante, então este post é a minha resposta.
Concordo que o controle de versões do dia a dia é trabalho para um agente de IA. É exatamente assim que eu trabalho. A diferença é que os comandos que meus agentes executam são do Jujutsu, não do Git. Depois de experimentar os dois jeitos, estou convencida de que, mesmo com a IA no comando, o Jujutsu oferece uma experiência de desenvolvimento muito melhor, e de que o tempo investido para aprendê-lo se paga rapidamente.
Antes de apresentar meus argumentos, vale esclarecer logo uma dúvida óbvia: a IA consegue mesmo lidar com o Jujutsu? Testei com Opus, GPT, Gemini e outros. Os modelos mais recentes já conhecem nativamente os conceitos básicos e os principais comandos do Jujutsu, e conseguem cuidar das operações do dia a dia sem carregar nenhuma skill extra. Dito isso, o Jujutsu não está tão integrado às ferramentas dos agentes quanto o Git, então é preciso alguma configuração para impedir que o agente volte ao Git sem avisar e para ensinar a ele um fluxo de trabalho adequado ao Jujutsu. Esta é a configuração que eu uso.
No Git, a unidade básica do histórico é o commit. O fluxo padrão é assim: você edita arquivos na working tree, escolhe os que quer e os adiciona ao índice, depois escreve uma mensagem e cria um commit. Só então algo entra no histórico. Um commit foi pensado para ser um produto acabado, algo feito com cuidado, e é por isso que o Git oferece o índice como staging area. Editar um arquivo e registrar essas alterações no histórico exige uma sequência longa e rígida de passos. É quase um ritual.
Então, mesmo quando você entrega o Git a uma IA, continua terminando cada tarefa com o pedido “faça o commit disso”. Peça qualquer operação no histórico n

title: Subscription Seats vs API Keys: Running the Break-Even Math
summary: Teams should choose between flat-rate subscription seats and pay-per-token API keys based on actual usage patterns rather than vendor comparison. Per-person token analysis reveals optimal pricing, while team averages hide the distribution and edge cases where subscription waste accumulates.
content:
A Hacker News thread comparing the value of Anthropic and OpenAI subscriptions turned into something more useful than a vendor scoreboard: people posting their actual usage and realizing they were paying the wrong way for it. Flat-rate seats and metered API keys are the same capability priced on two different axes, and most teams pick one by habit.
A subscription is a flat monthly fee per person with soft usage caps. An API key is pay-per-token with no ceiling. Does your usage pattern reward a fixed price or a variable one? That's the distinction that matters before you compare vendors—who gives more value per dollar is secondary.
Heavy, steady, interactive use favors seats. Someone coding against a model for six hours a day will blow past any flat fee's token-equivalent value, and the vendor pays for that. Bursty, automated, or embedded use favors the API: a feature that calls a model twice per user session doesn't need a seat, and more importantly, a seat can't be called from your backend anyway.
Teams buy seats for people who use the model twice a week, or run batch jobs on API keys that would have been free under a plan someone already pays for. Both are quiet, recurring waste that nobody's dashboard flags.
You don't need a model to decide this. You need last month's token counts per person, which every provider console exports.
seat_price = 100.00 # flat monthly plan, per person
blended_rate = 6.00 / 1_000_000 # your $ per token, input+output mixed
tokens = 18_000_000 # last month, one person, from your logs

api_cost = tokens * blended_rate
print(f"${api_cost:.2f} metered vs ${seat_price:.2f} seat")
print("buy the seat" if api_cost > seat_price else "stay on the API")

Run it per person, not as a team average. Averages hide the shape of the distribution - in my experience a few people generate the majority of tokens, and those are the only ones where a seat clearly wins.

title: Field notes from running small services
summary: A practical guide to running production services on single servers emphasizing security hardening, reversible deployments, and targeted observability. Key patterns include localhost-only app binding, health-check based monitoring, and avoiding over-engineering complexity with orchestration platforms.
content:
I keep a running list of the things I do on every small service I run. None of it is clever. All of it has saved me at least once. I wrote up the full setup in You probably do not need Kubernetes. These are the notes I actually come back to.
Before the app goes anywhere near a server, the server has to be safe to expose. No root login. Key-only SSH. A firewall open on 80, 443, and SSH, and nothing else. Something like fail2ban to cut down the noise.
The step people skip is disabling password authentication. Do it only after you have confirmed key login works in a second session. I have locked myself out doing it the fast way, and it is a bad hour.
One line, worth more than most of the architecture decisions I make:
ports:
  - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"

The app port is reachable only from the machine itself, so the reverse proxy is the only door in. If the proxy config breaks, you have a broken site, not an exposed service.
certbot renew --dry-run

Five seconds. If it fails, I want to know today rather than the morning a certificate expires and the site goes red.
If deploying feels dangerous, you avoid it, and then you ship one scary change. The fix is small and reversible deploys. On a push, run the tests, and if they pass, update the box. Keep secrets in the platform, never in the repo. Keep the previous version one step away.
A server you cannot see is a server you are guessing about. For a small service that means a health check that reflects real readiness, an external monitor that pages you when it stops answering, and logs you can read. That is enough. Collecting more than that, before there is a question to answer, is procrastination wearing a dashboard.
Kubernetes earns its keep when there are several services that scale independently, or a team that deploys without you, or a scheduler with real work to do. Until then it is a second job you volunteered for. I would rather run one box I understand than a cluster I have to look up.

title: What happens to a Shopify webhook when your endpoint goes down
summary: Shopify webhooks fail if endpoints don't respond within five seconds, with common integration failures occurring when work runs inside the request handler. The solution decouples receipt from delivery by immediately storing events and processing downstream after responding with success.
content:
I spent the last few months building a service that sits between Shopify or WooCommerce stores and the systems that consume their webhooks: ERPs, warehouse tools, accounting. Along the way I kept a list of the failure modes behind "an order never showed up" tickets. None of them are exotic, but most integrations I looked at handle only one or two.
Here is the list, with the fix I used for each.
The Shopify docs are direct about it: "If your app doesn't respond within five seconds, the delivery fails."
The common mistake is doing the real work inside the request: verify, parse, call the ERP, write to the warehouse system, then return 200. When the ERP is slow, Shopify records a failure even though your code finished the job, and a retry arrives for an order you already processed.
The fix is to split receiving from delivering. The endpoint does three things only: verify the signature, store the raw body, answer 200. Delivery to the ERP happens after the response.
@app.post("/webhooks/shopify")
async def shopify_webhook(request: Request):
    raw_body = await request.body()
    signature = request.headers.get("x-shopify-hmac-sha256", "")

    if not signature_ok(SHOPIFY_SECRET, raw_body, signature):
        return JSONResponse({"ok": False}, status_code=401)

    event_id = store_event(request.headers, raw_body)
    enqueue_delivery(event_id)
    return {"ok": True}

If your endpoint keeps failing, Shopify "retries failed webhook calls up to eight times in a four-hour period", and if failures persist, the subscription is removed.
In practice: a deploy breaks the endpoint on Friday evening. By Saturday morning every order event from that window is lost, and Shopify has stopped sending new ones. Nobody sees an error. Orders just stop arriving in the ERP.
Two things help:
Keep the receiving endpoint small and boring, so it is the last thing to break. It should not depend on the ERP being up.
Retry on your side, over a longer window than Shopify's. Once the event is stored

title: Delayed Webhook Retries: Idempotent Queue Workers Without Duplicate Deliveries
summary: Webhook retries should use message queues with per-event backoff timing rather than cron jobs, combined with idempotent workers that track processed events. This approach prevents duplicate fulfillment, charges, and partner API calls while maintaining durability and handling production concurrency.
content:
An e-commerce webhook retry can outlive the request that created it, and every order event needs its own backoff clock. Short answer: put delayed webhook retries on a queue, then make the worker idempotent because at-least-once delivery permits duplicate messages.
That choice optimizes the useful trade: accept a little queueing latency and one durable lookup per delivery rather than pay for duplicate fulfillment, duplicate email, or repeated partner calls. Cron is the wrong primitive for per-event timing. A retry due in 37 seconds should travel with that event, not wait for a scheduler that scans every pending order.
The queue alone doesn't solve duplicate processing.
At-least-once means the broker may deliver the same message again. The important word is may. A consumer can finish the business action and lose its chance to acknowledge, or two consumers can temporarily see equivalent work; either way, delivery and business completion aren't one indivisible operation. Retrying is correct behavior for the queue, while repeating the order-side effect is incorrect behavior for the application.
This is why a message ID is not merely useful logging context. Treat a stable event ID as an idempotency key and persist a processed-event record in the same transaction as the local state change. On another delivery, the worker checks that record and returns success without applying the change twice. If the outbound partner also accepts an idempotency key, forward the same stable value, but don't assume that removes the need for your own record.
The easy first version is usually a loop that polls a database table by next_attempt_at. It looks attractive in a notebook: one table, one query, no queue. Under production concurrency, though, that table becomes a scheduler, lease manager, retry counter, and contention point. The implementation has quietly started rebuilding queue semantics. A queue with delayed publishing keeps event-specific timing in the delivery system, while the app

title: Idempotency - "The customer clicked 'Pay' three times. How do you ensure they're charged only once?"
summary: Idempotency keys prevent duplicate charges when users retry payment requests by having servers cache and return previous responses for identical requests. This pattern is essential for payments, orders, and inventory operations where duplicate processing carries financial risk.
content:
Most know what idempotency is; very few can clearly explain why it's needed and how its actually implemented.
Imagine a payment system. The user clicks "Pay." The request reaches the server and is
response never reaches the user because of a network timeout,
What does the user do? They click "Pay" again.
Without idempotency, this retry can cause the API to:
Create multiple orders

Charge the customer duplicate payments

Deduct inventory more than once
Produce a very angry customer



The core issue: the client cannot tell the difference between "my request never arrived" and "my
 Both look identical from the client's side — a
Generate a unique Idempotency Key for each logical request (not each HTTP call — the same
First request with a given key → process it normally, then store the response alongside
the key.
Retry with the same key → the server recognizes it's already been handled, and simply
returns the previously stored response instead of processing the request again.
No duplicate processing, no matter how many times the client retries.
The core guarantee: Same request + same key = same result, every time.
Client                         Server
  │  POST /pay (Idempotency-Key: abc123)
  ├──────────────────────────────►
  │                               │  key "abc123" not seen before
  │                               │  → process payment
  │                               │  → store {key: abc123, response: {...}}
  │  ◄── 200 OK {charge_id: X}────┤
  │  (response lost in transit)   │
  │
  │  Retry: POST /pay (Idempotency-Key: abc123)
  ├──────────────────────────────►
  │                               │  key "abc123" already exists
  │                               │  → skip processing, return stored response
  │  ◄── 200 OK {charge_id: X}────┤   (same charge_id, no new charge)

Anywhere duplicate side effects are unacceptable:
Payment APIs
Order creation
Money transfers
Ticket booking
Inventory updates

title: Infrastructure was not where I started
summary: Low-level systems programming in C and shell scripting builds debugging instincts that transfer to infrastructure work despite changing technologies. Understanding the layers below your current work enables reasoning about failure modes rather than guessing when production systems break.
content:
Infrastructure was not where I started.
I started in C. Pointers, arrays, strings, then memory allocation, linked lists, and eventually a shell. For months the work was small and low level: read a line, parse it, fork, exec, wait. Debug a segfault until it finally made sense. Recompile.
At the time it did not feel like infrastructure. It felt like fighting the machine. The compiler disagreed with me constantly. Memory had to be handed back by hand. Almost nothing was convenient.
Then I moved into Linux administration, Docker, CI/CD, and running production systems. And I kept noticing that the hard part was familiar.
When a container exits with code 137, that is the OOM killer, and it helps that I once had to think about how memory is actually used. When a process will not die, signals stopped being mysterious back in the shell project. When a service will not start, reading the log and following the failure chain is the same skill as tracing why a pointer wrote to the wrong place.
The language changed. The habit did not. The habit is this: understand the layer below the one you work in, so that when something breaks you can reason about why instead of guessing.
That is the thing ALX actually gave me, more than any single technology. It made being lost normal, and it made me comfortable opening the box.
If you are in the middle of the low level work right now, and it feels disconnected from the jobs you want, this is what I would say. The specific skills transfer less than you expect. The instincts transfer more. And the instincts are the part nobody can take from you.
Still learning. Still running small things on a single box more often than not.

title: How to export any public Telegram channel to JSON and read it in English (no login, no bot token)
summary: A tool scrapes public Telegram channels via HTML web previews without API credentials by parsing posts and paginating through history. The approach avoids MTProto phone login requirements and enables AI-powered translation and summarization of non-English channels.
content:
A lot of useful information lives in Telegram channels: tech news, market commentary, local announcements. Much of it isn't in English. If you want to follow ten Russian or Ukrainian tech channels, copying posts into a translator one by one gets old fast.
The obvious options both have catches:
The official Telegram API (MTProto) needs an api_id from my.telegram.org and a login with your phone number. That's more setup than a quick export deserves, and it ties the scraper to your personal account.
The Bot API only delivers new posts from channels the bot has been added to. It has no way to read a channel's history.
There's a third option that needs neither: every public channel has a web preview at https://t.me/s/<channel>. It's plain HTML, about 20 posts per page, and it pages backwards with a ?before=<post id> parameter.
I built a small tool on top of it. Here is how it works, the problems I ran into, and how I added AI translation and summaries.
import re
import time

import httpx
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup


def parse_page(html: str):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
    posts = []
    for msg in soup.select(".tgme_widget_message[data-post]"):
        if "service_message" in msg.get("class", []):
            continue
        text_el = msg.select_one(".tgme_widget_message_text.js-message_text")
        if text_el:
            for br in text_el.find_all("br"):
                br.replace_with("\n")
        time_el = msg.select_one(".tgme_widget_message_date time")
        views_el = msg.select_one(".tgme_widget_message_views")
        posts.append({
            "id": int(msg["data-post"].split("/")[1]),
            "url": "https://t.me/" + msg["data-post"],
            "date": time_el["datetime"] if time_el else None,
            "text": text_el.get_text().strip() if text_el else "",
            "views": views_el.get_text(strip=True) if views_el else None,  # e.g. "15.4K"
        })
    more = soup.select_one("link[rel=prev]")  # href="/s/<channel>?b

title: You probably do not need Kubernetes
summary: Kubernetes introduces unnecessary complexity for small applications on single servers; most simple services need only Docker, reverse proxy, and basic hardening. A practical alternative uses VPS hosting with Nginx, automated certificates, and CI/CD-driven deployments.
content:
Every few months I talk to someone who wants to put a small app on Kubernetes. Usually the app is one container, a database, and a handful of users. Often it is not even in production yet.
Kubernetes is excellent at a specific job: running many services, across many machines, with a team that deploys independently. If that is not your situation, it is a large amount of complexity you are taking on for a problem you do not have.
Most of my services run on a single VPS, and this is roughly how I set one up.
Before anything runs, the server needs to be safe to expose. That means no root login, no password authentication, a firewall with only the ports I need, and something like fail2ban to cut down the noise. It is ten minutes of work, once.
The step people skip is disabling password authentication, because it is the one that can lock you out. Confirm your key login works in a second session before you close the first. I have gotten that wrong, and it is a bad hour.
I run almost everything in Docker. One detail matters more than the rest: I bind the app port to 127.0.0.1 instead of exposing it.
ports:
  - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"

That single choice means the container is never directly reachable from the internet. Only the reverse proxy in front of it can talk to it. If I misconfigure the proxy, the worst case is a broken site, not an open service.
Nginx does three jobs for me. It proxies to the app, it terminates HTTPS, and it is the layer I edit when routing changes or a new domain shows up. Certbot handles the certificates, including the renewal timer, so I am not the renewal timer.
The one check I run on every new server is certbot renew --dry-run. If that fails, I want to know today rather than the morning a certificate expires.

title: Ingesting Source Code and Scripted Schema Without a Database Connection
summary: Corporate AI 365 analyzes source code and database schemas without requiring live database connections, enabling secure code reviews for regulated industries like healthcare and finance by providing AI systems with code structure while keeping customer data and PII inaccessible.
content:
A production incident lands on a Toronto engineering team's desk at 2 p.m. on a Tuesday. The on-call developer is on vacation. The remaining senior engineer is in a design review. Someone from customer support has already escalated it twice. Before anyone writes a line of diagnostic code, a security architect is going to ask one question about any tool you bring in to help: what does it connect to?
That question gets harder, not easier, when the tool in question claims to understand your codebase well enough to point at a file, a class, a line. The instinct is to assume it needs a live connection string to your production database to do that. It does not, and the distinction is worth walking through properly, because it is the first thing that should end — or extend — a security review.
Corporate AI 365 ingests two things: your source code, pulled through a connector to GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps, and a scripted database schema — a DDL export that your own team generates and commits, not a live connection the platform opens itself. No rows. No connection string. No driver pointed at a production host.
This is a meaningful constraint, not an oversight. A scripted schema gives the model table structures, foreign keys, indexes, constraints — everything it needs to reason about how an order record relates to a payments table, or why a nullable column is producing a downstream null-reference error. It does not give it a single customer's data, a single transaction, a single PII field. The model reasons about shape, never content.
For a payments company near Bay Street, or a healthcare SME in Vancouver handling PHI under provincial privacy law, that distinction is the whole conversation with legal. You are not asking anyone to approve a third party reading live patient or transaction data. You are asking them to approve a tool that reads code your developers already wrote and a schema export your developers already control the contents of.

title: Inside OpenAI's Invisible Text Watermarking for the EU AI Act
summary: OpenAI's textGrain embeds invisible watermarks in text output by subtly biasing word choices during generation to comply with EU AI Act transparency rules, matching Anthropic's similar approach for Claude deployed earlier in 2026.
content:
On October 5, 2026, OpenAI announced that ChatGPT and Codex will start embedding invisible watermarks into their text output for EU users. The feature is called textGrain, and it exists because of one law: the EU AI Act.
If you build on top of OpenAI's models, or you're just curious how "invisible AI watermarking" actually works under the hood, here's a breakdown.
The EU AI Act's transparency rules took effect on August 2, 2026. They require AI companies to mark AI-generated content in ways that can be detected, not necessarily by the naked eye, but by a tool built for the job.
OpenAI put it plainly: "The EU AI Act's transparency rules require AI companies to mark AI-generated content."
This isn't OpenAI being proactive out of goodwill. It's compliance. Which, if you've followed this space, is worth noting, because OpenAI has had a working text watermarking technique sitting on the shelf for roughly a year, and had previously chosen not to ship it over concerns about bias against non-native English speakers and how easily it could be defeated. The EU AI Act appears to have forced the decision.
Anthropic shipped something similar for Claude back in August, for the same regulatory reason. This is quickly becoming table stakes for any model provider operating in the EU.
Here's the part developers usually want to know: it doesn't touch pixels, metadata, or hidden Unicode characters. It lives in the words themselves.
From OpenAI's own explanation, the watermark works by subtly shaping the model's word choices during generation. Every time the model predicts the next token, there's usually a cluster of statistically similar options it could pick. textGrain uses a secret key to quietly bias which of those near-equal choices gets selected, across hundreds of these micro-decisions in a single response.
The result: a pattern invisible to a human reader, but detectable by a tool that knows the key.

title: Stop detecting AI content. Start signing it at the source
summary: Cryptographic provenance signing is more reliable than watermarking for proving AI-generated content authenticity because it creates tamper-evident signatures external to content, whereas watermarks degrade with edits and offer only probabilistic detection.
content:
Every few months someone ships a new way to detect AI-generated text or images, and every few months someone else shows how to strip it. Paraphrase the text, crop or re-encode the image, and the hidden signal gets weaker or disappears. Detection is a cat and mouse game, and the mouse only needs to win once.
There is a calmer way to think about this. Instead of asking "can I prove this was made by AI?", ask "can I prove where this came from and that nobody changed it since?" That is provenance, and it is a much easier problem to engineer.




Watermark / detector
Signed provenance




Where it lives
hidden inside the content
a small record next to the content


What it claims
"this probably came from model X"
"this exact file came from source Y at time T"


Survives edits?
degrades with paraphrase, crops, re-encoding
any edit breaks the signature, which is the point


Failure mode
silent false negatives and false positives
missing or invalid signature, clearly visible


Who can check
usually only the vendor
anyone with the public key



A watermark tries to make the content itself carry the evidence. Provenance keeps the evidence outside the content and makes it cryptographically checkable. When the content changes, you do not get a fuzzy score, you get a clear "this is not the file that was signed".
You do not need a platform to try this. Hash the output, sign the hash with a key the producer controls, and ship a tiny manifest with it.
import hashlib, json, time
from nacl.signing import SigningKey  # pip install pynacl

key = SigningKey.generate()          # keep this secret, publish key.verify_key
content = open("report.txt", "rb").read()

manifest = {
    "sha256": hashlib.sha256(content).hexdigest(),
    "producer": "summarizer-v3",
    "model": "model-name-and-version",
    "created": int(time.time()),
}
payload = json.dumps(manifest, sort_keys=True).encode()
signature = key.sign(payload).signature.hex()

title: How Business Call Routing Systems Work: A Beginner's Guide

content:
When you build or launch a small product, early user and client communications are dead simple: your phone rings, you pick it up, answer a question, and solve a problem.
Why Call Routing Matters
Concurrency limits: A standard physical device can handle only one active audio stream without placing someone on hold.


Context fragmentation: Call details remain stranded in private device logs instead of syncing with a CRM or incident tracking database.


Resource mismatch: High-priority buyers wait behind general billing questions, or senior engineers answer basic password-reset calls.



Every routed call passes through an ingress pipeline consisting of three stages: Ingress & Caller Identification, Rule Evaluation, and Dispatching.
How can we actually implement Call Routing?
Interactive Voice Response (IVR): The caller interacts with an automated voice menu using DTMF (touch-tone keypads) or speech-to-text recognition:


Department-Based Routing splits inbound traffic across functional boundaries.


Time-Based (Schedules & Business Hours): Evaluates calls against a time condition. After Hours & Weekends are routed directly to an on-call rotation, voicemail-to-ticket system, or an emergency escalation tree.


Call Forwarding: If a desktop softphone or primary extension fails to establish a session within a configurable timeout, the engine issues a forward rule to an external mobile number or backup device.

And when nobody answers, reliable systems always have an else branch. When all endpoints are busy, offline, or fail to pick up within the designated TTL (Time-To-Live), failover logic kicks in.
A phone conversation shouldn't be an ephemeral event that disappears when someone hangs up.

We’ve all been there: staring at a screen for two hours trying to fix a bug, only to realize we missed a single semicolon or misunderstood the logic completely. 
Writing clean, maintainable code isn't just about knowing syntax or memorizing framework tricks. It’s about building everyday habits that streamline your workflow and save your sanity.

When facing a tricky bug or trying a new library, our first instinct is often to spend hours tinkering or endlessly searching stack traces online. 
While experimenting is great, taking 5 minutes to read the official documentation often saves you hours of frustration. 
Docs give you the intended context behind the tool.
You discover built-in methods you didn't even know existed.

Computers don't care if your variable is named x or userAuthenticationStatus. But your teammates—and future you 6 months from now—definitely do.

const d = new Date();
const x = users.filter(u => u.a && u.age > 18);
✅ Clean & self-explanatory:
const currentDate = new Date();
const activeAdultUsers = users.filter(user => user.isActive && user.age > 18);
"Any fool can write code that a computer can understand. Good programmers write code that humans can understand." — Martin Fowler
Pushing a massive Git commit with the message "fixed bugs and added stuff" is a nightmare for code reviews and version control.
Keep commits atomic (one feature or fix per commit).
Write clear, imperative commit messages (git commit -m "Add user validation to signup form").
Push early and push often.
This makes debugging with git blame or reverting broken changes infinitely easier!
Randomly changing lines of code hoping the error goes away is called "Shotgun Debugging"—and it rarely works.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass. Touch Grass Birder is a bird call identifier that runs entirely on your own machine. title: How eBPF Actually Runs Inside the Linux Kernel: The Verifier, JIT, and BPF Maps
summary: eBPF programs execute in a sandboxed kernel environment verified by a static analyzer and compiled to native instructions via JIT compilation, not through an interpreter, preventing kernel panics from unsafe operations.
content:
How eBPF Actually Runs Inside the Linux Kernel: The Verifier, JIT, and BPF Maps


If you ask most developers how eBPF works, you usually get one of two answers:
"It is a tiny virtual machine inside Linux, like a JVM for the kernel."
"It is a way to run custom C code in the kernel without writing a kernel module."
Both explanations miss the fundamental architecture. 
eBPF does not run inside an interpreter loop at runtime, and it definitely does not allow arbitrary C execution. If you could execute arbitrary C in kernel space, a single null pointer dereference or off-by-one loop would panic your entire operating system.
Instead, eBPF is an in-kernel sandboxed execution engine governed by an unforgiving static verifier, compiled to native machine instructions via a Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler, and bridged to user space through lockless, memory-mapped data structures.
Here is the exact mechanical journey of an eBPF program: from user-space bytecode compilation, through the kernel's symbolic execution verifier, down to native CPU execution on kernel hooks.
Before touching the kernel, your high-level C or Rust code is compiled by LLVM/Clang targeting the bpf backend (clang -target bpf -O2). 
The output is not x86 or ARM assembly. It is 64-bit eBPF bytecode designed around an idealized RISC register machine:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       eBPF Register Architecture                      |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  Register  | Purpose                                                  |
+------------+----------------------------------------------------------+
|  R0        | Function return value & exit code to kernel hook         |
|  R1 - R5   | Function arguments passed to in-kernel BPF helpers       |
|  R6 - R9   | Callee-saved registers (preserved across helper calls)  |
|  R10       | Read-only frame pointer to 512-byte stack frame          |
+----------

zh.summary: eBPF 程序在沙箱化内核环境中执行，由静态分析器验证，通过 JIT 编译为本地指令而非解释器，防止不安全操作导致内核崩溃。

title: Your AIs don't talk to each other. Here's how to give them one shared memory in 2 minutes
summary: Using the Model Context Protocol, developers can connect multiple AI assistants to a shared remote memory server, enabling context to persist across tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor without manual copy-pasting.
content:
Monday, 9:14 pm. I tell ChatGPT about a new client: Claire Morel, Atelier Lumen, showcase website, €4,800, delivery end of November. She wants a clean look. No purple.
Tuesday morning, I open Claude to write her proposal.
Claude has never heard of Claire.
So I paste the context again. And again on Wednesday, in another chat. And again in Cursor. If you use more than one AI assistant, you know this tax: every assistant has its own memory, and none of them share it. You are the copy-paste layer between your AIs.
This post fixes that in about two minutes, with no code and nothing to install.
outside your assistants


The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an assistant call external tools. Most people use it for GitHub or Notion. But a tool can also be a memory: a server with store, search and recall functions.
Host that server at a URL (a remote MCP server), connect every assistant to it, and something simple happens:
What Claude saves, ChatGPT can find. What ChatGPT learns, Cursor already knows.
One memory, all your AIs.

Every memory, grouped by client and project. (The app UI is in French for now: it's built in France.)

claude.ai → Settings → Connectors

Name: Pryzm, URL: https://pryzm-memory.com/mcp → Add


Connect → sign in (OAuth)
Works on the free plan (one custom connector), web and desktop.
ChatGPT connects to remote MCP servers through Developer mode (beta, web, paid plans).
chatgpt.com → Settings → Apps


Advanced settings → turn on Developer mode

Create an app with https://pryzm-memory.com/mcp, authorize with OAuth
In a new chat: + → Developer mode → enable the app
Each assistant gets its own token. Revoke one, the others keep working.
